[p. 346]

The opening of the surah with the vocative address to the Prophet (ﷺ) is an alert that what follows concerns the Prophet (ﷺ) and the community, and because the occasion of revelation was among his concerns.

The interrogative in His words ﴿Why do you forbid﴾ is used with the meaning of negation: there is no reason that should move you to forbid yourself what Allah has made lawful for you. For when he (ﷺ) committed himself not to return to what had passed from him, whether by an oath or without an oath, he intended to abstain from it in the future, aiming thereby to reassure his wives, who had banded together against him because of their intense jealousy. That is, their jealousy is not something whose observance is obligatory in companionship, if it was over matters that did not infringe on their rights, nor is it part of one wife's honouring of her husband if the other was unable to honour him in the same way on some days.

This points to the principle that defines which jealousy is to be observed and which is not.

The verb ﴿tuharrimu﴾ (you forbid) is used with the meaning: you make what has been made lawful for you unlawful, that is, you forbid it upon yourself, like His words, exalted is He, ﴿except what Israel made unlawful for himself﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 93]. Its indicator is His words here, ﴿what Allah has made lawful for you﴾.

The meaning of prohibition here is not the attribution of the act to its being unlawful, as in His words, ﴿Say: who has forbidden the adornment of Allah which He brought forth for His servants, and the good things of provision?﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 32], and His words, ﴿they make it lawful one year and forbid it another year﴾ [al-Tawbah: 37]. For the tafʿīl form (the intensive/causative verbal pattern) comes with the meaning of making something into a certain state, as one says: widen this door, and it also comes with the meaning of bringing a thing into being in a certain condition, as one says to the tailor: widen the collar of the robe.

No one would imagine from it that you changed its permissibility into prohibition for the people or for yourself. It is strange that the words of al-Kashshāf say: no one has the right to forbid what Allah has made lawful, because Allah only made it lawful for a benefit He knew in its being made lawful, etc.

The form of the present tense in His words ﴿you forbid﴾ is used because he had brought about a renewed prohibition.

So the clause ﴿you seek﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the pronoun in ﴿you forbid﴾. Thus the wonder falls upon the content of both clauses, like His words, ﴿do not consume usury, doubled and redoubled﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 130]. And in the use of the relative pronoun in His words ﴿what Allah has made lawful for you﴾ there is, in the relative clause (ṣilah), an indication of the reason for the ruling, which is that what Allah has made lawful for His servant ought to be enjoyed by him so long as there does not arise what requires its cessation, such as harm or illness, because partaking of it is thankfulness to Allah and acknowledgment of His blessing and of one's need for it.

[p. 347]

In His words ﴿seeking the pleasure of your wives﴾ there is an excuse for the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding what he did, in that he intended by it a good, namely gaining the pleasure of the wives, since that is easier for living together with them. It also conveys that such pleasure is not worth much, because the jealousy arose merely from some of them opposing others, and this is something that disrupts the goodness of companionship among them. So Allah informed him that this effort is outweighed by the fact that forbidding what Allah has made lawful for him leads to cutting off many of the means of thanking Allah when partaking of His blessings, and that this ought to be eliminated from the conduct of the community.

It is concluded with the clause ﴿And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾ to console the Prophet (ﷺ) from the distress of this reproach. That is: and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful toward you, like His words, ﴿Allah pardon you! Why did you grant them leave?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 43].

[p. 348]

This is an explanatory resumptive clause (istinaf bayani), through which God clarified for His Prophet ﷺ that he has latitude to release himself from what he had committed himself to forbidding upon himself. This refers to what God legislated concerning the expiation (kaffara) for oaths (yamin). God therefore instructed him to take advantage of this concession in the expiation for oaths, which is prescribed for the whole community. Among the effects of the ruling of this verse is what the Prophet ﷺ said to the delegation of 'Abd al-Qays after they asked him for mounts and he swore that he would not carry them, since he did not have anything to mount them on. Then a few camels from the sadaqa (alms) were brought to him, and he said to them: "By God, I do not swear an oath and then see something other than it as better, except that I expiate my oath and do what is better."

The opening of the report with the particle of confirmation (harf al-tahqiq) places the Prophet ﷺ in the position of one who does not know that God had made the release from oaths obligatory through the verse of expiation, on the basis that he had not taken the concession out of reverence for the oath. God informed him that taking up the expiation holds no shortcoming for him in this matter, for the expiation suffices to fulfil the glorification of an oath by God, and nothing beyond it is required. This is the statement of God the Exalted in the story of Ayyub (﴿And take in your hand a bundle of grass and strike with it, and do not break your oath﴾ [Sad 38:44]), as we mentioned in its tafsir. The word (faradha) means "to specify," and from it is the saying of God the Exalted (﴿a portion specified﴾ [al-Nisa 4:7]). It is said: "He specified for him a share in the allowance," and the meaning is: God has clarified for you the release from your oaths.

Know that if the Prophet ﷺ had made no vow in that incident except that he committed himself not to return to drinking something at the house of some of his wives on a day other than her turn, or if there was a promise that he would forbid Mariyah to himself without an oath according to the other narration, then that was not an oath. God's command to him to expiate for his oath is then either because that operates in the manner of an oath, since he only promised this to reassure the hearts of his wives, so it is a commitment toward them, and thereby it is attached to the oath. Abu Hanifa took this view, while Malik did not regard it as an oath or a vow. He said in the Muwatta': the meaning of the saying of the Messenger of God ﷺ, "Whoever vows to disobey God, let him not disobey Him," is that a man vows to walk to Syria or to Egypt, or to do something that is not an act of obedience to God, if he speaks to so-and-so. There is nothing upon him in that if he speaks to him, because there is no obedience to God in these matters. But if he swears, saying: "By God, I will not eat this food and I will not wear this garment," then upon him is only the expiation of an oath. End quote.

It has been disputed whether the Prophet ﷺ expiated for that oath.

So the release (tahillah), according to this interpretation, in the view of Malik, is: God making the one who has committed himself to the like of this to be free from the obligation of what he committed himself to. That is, He makes the release from his oath binding.

According to Abu Hanifa, it is what God legislated of release from oaths through expiations, even if the Prophet ﷺ had uttered an oath at that time not to return. So the release from the oath is, according to all, the expiation.

The clause (﴿And God is your Mawla (protector)﴾) is a concluding phrase (tadhyil) for the clause (﴿God has indeed specified for you the release from your oaths﴾). The mawla is the wali (guardian), that is the helper and the one who manages the affairs attributed to him. Here it is a metaphor (kinaya) for the Compassionate and the Facilitator, as in His saying the Exalted (﴿God intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship﴾ [al-Baqara 2:185]).

Following it is the clause (﴿and He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise﴾), meaning: the All-Knowing of what sets you right, so He guides you to what is correct, rightly guided and upright; and He is the All-Wise regarding what He legislates, meaning He applies His rulings according to wisdom. Wisdom is giving actions what their realities require, without illusions and imaginings.

The jurists of Islam have differed concerning one who forbids himself something that God has made lawful for him, with many opinions, which al-Qurtubi reduced to eighteen opinions, some of which overlap with others according to differences in conditions and intentions, so that they return to seven.

The first: nothing is binding upon him, whether the forbidden thing is a wife or something else. This is the view of al-Sha'bi, Masruq, and Rabi'a among the Successors, and Asbagh ibn al-Faraj from the companions of Malik said it.

The second: an expiation like the expiation for an oath is required. It is narrated from Abu Bakr, 'Umar, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, 'A'isha, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and al-Awza'i and al-Shafi'i in one of his two opinions said the same. This accords with the apparent meaning of the verse in His saying (﴿God has indeed specified for you the release from your oaths﴾).

The third: nothing is binding upon him regarding other than a wife. As for the wife, it is said: if he has consummated the marriage with her, the prohibition is three (divorces), and if he has not consummated it, he is believed concerning what he intended. This is the view of al-Hasan, al-Hakam, and Malik in the well-known position. It is also said that it is three divorces, whether he consummated the marriage or not. It is attributed to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Zayd ibn Thabit, and Abu Hurayra. Ibn Abi Layla said it, and it is from 'Abd al-Malik ibn al-Majishun in al-Mabsut. It is also said it is one irrevocable divorce. It is attributed to Zayd ibn Thabit and Hammad ibn Sulayman, and Ibn Khuwayz Mandad attributed it to Malik, though this is not the well-known position from him. It is also said: one revocable divorce in regard to the wife absolutely. It is attributed to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, so this is a restriction of what was narrated from him in the second opinion. It was said by al-Zuhri, 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Abi Salama, and Ibn al-Majishun. Al-Shafi'i, in one of his two opinions, said: if he intends divorce, then upon him is what he intended of its numbers; otherwise it is one revocable divorce. It is also said: it is three in the case of the wife with whom he has consummated the marriage, and one in the case of the one with whom he has not consummated it, without intention being considered.

The fourth: Abu Hanifa and his companions said: if he intends by the word "haram" (forbidden) the zihar (a pre-Islamic form of divorce by likening the wife to a forbidden relative), then what he intended applies. If he intends divorce, then it is one irrevocable divorce, unless he intended three. If he did not intend anything, it is an oath, and upon him is an expiation; if he refuses it, he is a mu'lli (one who has sworn to abstain from intercourse).

The Prophet's ﷺ prohibition of his concubine Mariyah upon himself is also of the kind of forbidding someone something that God made lawful for him other than a wife, because Mariyah was not his wife but rather his slave-woman. So the ruling of His saying (﴿God has indeed specified for you the release from your oaths﴾) applies to the matter of forbidding Mariyah, whether by oath or without oath, with no distinction.

"Tahillah" is on the pattern of taf'ila, from hallala, meaning he made the act lawful. Its original form is tahillah, and the two lams were assimilated. It is a verbal noun learned by hearing (masdar sama'i), because the ha' at its end is not by analogy, since no letter was removed from it so that the ha' would be a compensation for it, like tazkiya; but it is common in speech, like ta'illa.

**[Page 350]**

﴿And when the Prophet confided to one of his wives a statement. Then when she informed [another] of it, and Allah disclosed it to him, he made known part of it and ignored part. Then when he informed her of it, she said, "Who told you this?" He said, "The All-Knowing, the All-Aware informed me."﴾

This is a reminder and an admonition concerning what occurred during those two incidents. After the matter of the legislation relevant to the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning what he had made forbidden to himself from them had been concluded, the course of speech was turned back toward it.

It is joined (ma'tuf) to the sentence ﴿O Prophet, why do you forbid what Allah has made lawful for you?﴾ [al-Tahrim: 1], with the implied verb "remember" (wadhkur).

What the preceding verse indicated implicitly has been repeated, through what this verse contains, in a different style, so that upon it may be built what it contains of lessons, admonitions, good manners, nobility of character, alerting and warning.

These verses therefore comprise twenty of these meanings. The first is what is contained in His saying ﴿to one of his wives﴾.

The second: His saying ﴿Then when she informed [another] of it﴾.

The third: ﴿and Allah disclosed it to him﴾.

The fourth: ﴿he made known part of it﴾.

The fifth: ﴿and ignored part﴾.

The sixth: ﴿She said, "Who told you this?"﴾.

The seventh: ﴿He said, "The All-Knowing, the All-Aware informed me."﴾.

The eighth, ninth and tenth: ﴿If you two repent to Allah﴾ [al-Tahrim: 4] through ﴿then Allah is his Protector﴾ [al-Tahrim: 4].

The eleventh, twelfth and thirteenth: ﴿and Gabriel, and the righteous among the believers, and the angels﴾ [al-Tahrim: 4].

The fourteenth and fifteenth: ﴿It may be that his Lord, if he divorces you, will substitute for him wives﴾ [al-Tahrim: 5].

The sixteenth: ﴿better than you﴾ [al-Tahrim: 5].

The seventeenth: ﴿submissive [Muslim women]﴾ [al-Tahrim: 5], etc.

The eighteenth: ﴿traveling [women]﴾ [al-Tahrim: 5].

The nineteenth: ﴿previously married and virgins﴾ [al-Tahrim: 5]. Their explanation will come at the commentary on each verse of them.

**[Page 351]**

The twentieth: the mention of Hafsah, or others, under the designation ﴿one of his wives﴾ without naming her is of the sufficiency in reproach by mentioning what makes one sense that she is the intended one for blame.

The Prophet (ﷺ) informed her that he knew of her divulging the statement by a command from Allah, so that he could build upon it the admonition and discipline, for Allah did not make him aware of her divulging it except for a noble purpose.

The "statement" (hadith) was what occurred from the Prophet's (ﷺ) seclusion with his slave-girl Mariyah, and what passed between him and Hafsah, and his saying to Hafsah, "She is forbidden to me," and "Do not inform 'Aishah." The two were close friends. Allah informed His Prophet (ﷺ) that Hafsah had informed 'Aishah of what he had confided to her.

The conjunction "and" (waw) links one narrative to another, because the story of Hafsah's divulging the secret is not the story of the Prophet's (ﷺ) forbidding to himself some of what had been made lawful to him.

The scholars did not differ that the one to whom the Prophet (ﷺ) confided the statement was Hafsah, and it will come that the one informed by her was 'Aishah. In the Sahih, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "I remained for a year wanting to ask 'Umar ibn al-Khattab about a verse, but I could not ask him out of awe of him, until he set out for pilgrimage. I went out with him, and when he returned, at some point on the road, I said, 'O Commander of the Believers, who are the two who conspired against the Messenger of Allah among his wives?' He said, 'They are Hafsah and 'Aishah,' and he related the story in its entirety."

The original application of the term "hadith" to speech is metaphorical, since it is derived from hadathan (occurrence), so that what occurs is the act and the like; it became widespread until it became the literal meaning for the report about it, and its application to the incident became the metaphor, so the state of its original usage and employment was reversed.

**(Asarra)** means: to inform of something one wants concealed from someone other than the informant; or to ask him not to divulge something that took place between them, even if it was not a report. This is when the report or the action is one whose spreading is not desired, so its speaker says it secretly. Secrecy (sirr) is the opposite of openness (jahr). Allah said: ﴿He knows what you conceal and what you disclose﴾ [al-Taghabun: 4]. Thus asarra came to be used in the sense of enjoining non-divulgence, i.e., non-disclosure. Allah said: ﴿Then Joseph kept it hidden within himself and did not reveal it to them﴾ [Yusuf: 77].

**Asarra** is a verb derived from sirr (secret), the hamzah in it being causative, i.e., he made it possessor of a secret. It is said: asarra fi nafsihi, when he concealed his secret. It is said: asarra ilayhi, when he told him a secret, as if he "delivered" it to him. It is said: asarra lahu, when he kept a matter for his sake, and that is usually in the concealment of evil. Asarra bi-kadha, i.e., he informed with a secret report, when he placed something hidden. In the proverb: "He sips quietly while gulping" (yusirru hasawan fi irtighaa).

**(﴿Bad'i azwajihi﴾)** ("one of his wives") is Hafsah bint 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. She is designated without her name out of dignity, since the aim is not the identification of persons; rather, what is meant is knowledge of the point of the story and what is in it that should be avoided or emulated. Likewise, the omission of identifying the one informed of the statement, who is 'Aishah.

Hafsah is mentioned by the title "his wives" to indicate that the Prophet (ﷺ) placed his secret in its proper place, because the people most worthy of knowing a man's secret is his wife. In that there is an implicit rebuke of her for divulging his secret, because it is incumbent upon a woman to guard her husband's secret when he commands her to guard it, or when it is of the kind he would want guarded.

This is the first of the disciplinary meanings we mentioned above.

**Nabba'a** (with doubling) is synonymous with **anba'a** (with hamzah), and both mean "informed." His saying ﴿Then when he informed her of it, she said, "Who told you this?" He said, "The All-Knowing, the All-Aware informed me."﴾ combines both.

It has been said: "The secret is a trust," meaning that divulging it is betrayal.

In the hadith of Umm Zar' there is among their ancient Arab customs: "The eleventh woman said: 'The slave-girl of Abu Zar'. What of the slave-girl of Abu Zar'? She does not spread our talk, nor does she shake out our provisions.'"

The sayings of the wise and the poets on secrets and guarding them are too numerous to count. This is the second of the disciplinary meanings we mentioned.

The meaning of ﴿and Allah disclosed it to him﴾ is "made him aware of it," and it is derived from **zuhur** in the sense of overcoming.

The word "disclosure" (izhar) is borrowed for "informing" (iṭla'), because Allah's making His Prophet (ﷺ) aware of the secret between Hafsah and 'Aishah was a victory for him over them in what they had plotted. So the particular state of the conspiracy of Hafsah and 'Aishah to learn the Prophet's (ﷺ) secret, and his knowledge of that, was likened to the state of one who overcomes another, and the other is overcome and his affair is exposed. So the "disclosure" here is from zuhur in the sense of victory, and it is not from zuhur as the opposite of concealment, because it does not take the preposition "over" ('ala) in that sense.

The pronoun in ('alayhi) refers either to the informing derived from "she informed him" (nabba'at bihi), or to the statement, with an implied noun indicated by "she informed him." Its meaning: Allah disclosed it to him concerning its divulging.

This is an alert to Allah's care for His Messenger (ﷺ) and His support of him, because informing him of what he had no knowledge of, but which concerns him, is care and sincere counsel for him.

This is the essential meaning of the third of the meanings the verses comprise that we mentioned above.

The first object of **'arrafa** is omitted, because the sentence indicates it: i.e., "he made her aware of part of it," meaning part of what Allah had made him aware of, and he ignored informing her of part of it. The statement contains several matters: the Prophet's (ﷺ) seclusion with his concubine Mariyah, his forbidding her to himself, his consuming honey in the house of Zaynab, his vow to avoid returning to such a thing, and perhaps something was interspersed in it, such as a description of Hafsah's suddenly coming upon it, or boasting that she was able to relieve them of his inclination toward Mariyah. The Prophet (ﷺ) made her aware of this only so that he might make her stand over her transgression of the obligation of good manners in guarding her husband's secret.

This is the fourth of the meanings I earlier indicated.

The Messenger's (ﷺ) ignoring to inform his wife of part of the statement she divulged is from the nobility of his character (ﷺ) in rebuking the one who divulged it and disciplining her, since the purpose is attained by making her aware of some of what she divulged, so she becomes certain that Allah is jealous over it.

Sufyan said: "Overlooking has always been the act of the noble." Al-Hasan said: "No noble person has ever pressed to the utmost," and he did not exceed the intended point by turning the rebuke from reproach into censure.

This is the fifth of the purposes of mentioning this statement, as we indicated above.

Her saying ﴿Who told you this?﴾ indicates her confidence that 'Aishah would not divulge her secret, and she knew that the Messenger (ﷺ) had no means of knowing this except through 'Aishah or through revelation, so she sought to verify one of the two possibilities.

**[Page 354]**

The interrogation is genuine, and you may take it as an expression of wonder at his knowledge of that.

In this is sufficient evidence of her awakening to the fact that divulging her husband's secret was a grave moral lapse, which the intensity of her closeness to 'Aishah, and her excessive delight at the forbidding of Mariyah for their sake, had veiled her from observing. So she could not restrain herself from announcing it to her intimate friend and supporter. Had she remembered, it would have become clear to her that the requirement of keeping her husband's secret outweighs the requirement of informing her friend, for the ties of marriage are stronger than the ties of friendship, and the duty of sincerity to the Messenger of Allah is higher than the virtue of sincerity to one's close companions.

This is the sixth of the meanings of the good manners contained in the story, which we summarized above.

The choosing of the two descriptions ﴿the All-Knowing, the All-Aware﴾ here instead of the proper name is for what they contain of reminder of what people must know: Allah's comprehensive encompassment of everything in knowledge and awareness.

**Al-'Alim** (the All-Knowing): one of great knowledge. Among His names, it indicates the most perfect knowledge, i.e., knowledge that encompasses every object of knowledge.

**Al-Khabir** (the All-Aware) is more specific than al-'Alim, since it is derived from **khabir al-shay'** when one comprehends its meanings and hidden depths; hence it is said: "khabartuhu," i.e., I tested him and penetrated the inner aspects of his affair. Ibn Burjan, with a dammed b and a doubled j, said in his explanation of the Names: "The difference between khabr and 'ilm and other things indicating the attribute of knowledge is that you recognize the attainment of benefit from a certain direction; add that to the attribute and name the benefit by the direction from which it was obtained. When it is obtained from a place of presence, it is called witnessing (mushahadah), and the one characterized by it is the witness (shahid) and the Witness (shahid). Likewise, if you obtain it through hearing or sight, the one characterized by it is the Hearer (sami') and the Seer (basir). Likewise, if it is obtained through knowledge or a sign, it is 'ilm, and the one characterized by it is the knower ('alim) and the All-Knowing ('Alim). And if it is obtained through uncovering the apparent of what is tested from its inner through trial, examination, experiment or announcement, then it is khabar, and the one named by it is al-Khabir." End of quote. Al-Ghazali said in al-Maqsad al-Asna: "Knowledge, when it is applied to hidden inner things, is called khibrah, and its possessor is called khabir." End.

Thus it becomes clear that the pairing of the attribute "al-'Alim" with the attribute "al-Khabir" is an allusion that Allah knew the inner intention of the one addressing (the wife) and what she intended by divulging the secret to the other.

**[Page 355]**

From this response there results instruction for her that Allah makes His Messenger (ﷺ) aware of what is hidden whenever He wills, as He said: ﴿The Knower of the unseen; He does not disclose His unseen to anyone﴾ [al-Jinn: 26], ﴿except whom He has approved of among messengers﴾ [al-Jinn: 27], and as an alert to what she had concealed of the matter.

This is the seventh of the good manners of these verses.

Know that **nabba'a** and **anba'a** are synonyms, both meaning "informed," and that their proper usage is transitivity to one object, because of the transitive hamzah or doubling in them. Though no unaugmented verb for them has been heard, and it is among what has become obsolete in their speech, being dispensed with by the verb 'alima. Most often they are transitive to what goes beyond the object by a prepositional particle, as in: nabba'tu bihi (I informed him of it). The preposition may be omitted, so they take two objects, as in His saying here ﴿Who told you this?﴾, i.e., "of this," and in the verse of al-Farazdaq:

*"I was informed, 'Abd Allah, that the noble clients of the plain have become ... of the pure of their lineage."*

Sibawayh interpreted it as omission of the particle.

They may also be made to imply the meaning of "know" ('alima), so they are transitive to three objects, as in the verse of al-Nabigha:

*"I was informed of Zur'ah, and foolishness, as its name suggests, brings me strange poems."*

Because of the frequency of this usage, it was thought to be a meaning of the two verbs, and the implication was overlooked. Hence the attaching of them to 'alima is attributed to Sibawayh, al-Farisi and al-Jurjani. Al-Farra' attached khabbara and akhbara, and the Kufans attached haddatha.

Zakariyya al-Ansari (Zakariyya al-Ansari) said: The construction of this verb with a double object is not heard in the speech of the Arabs (in the sense of taking three objects) except when it is in the passive voice.

The majority of readers recited ʿarrafa with the doubled rāʾ (shadda). Al-Kisa'i recited ʿarafa with a single rāʾ (takhfif), meaning he made known some of it (ʿalima baʿḍahu). This is a metaphor (kināya) for requital: that is, he requited her for some of it, namely her divulging it, with blame or with divorce, according to the report that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) divorced Hafsa, though this report is not authentic. The threat is sometimes expressed metaphorically by the verb "to know" and similar, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those are the ones whose hearts God knows what is in them﴾ [al-Nisa': 63]. Also the saying of the Arabs to one who has done wrong: "I will surely know this about you," and your saying: "Indeed I have known what you did."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 66, verse 4:

Page 356
﴿If you two repent to Allah, your hearts have indeed inclined (to that which He disapproves). But if you cooperate against him, then indeed Allah is his protector, and Jibril and the righteous among the believers, and after that the angels are (his) supporters.﴾

This is a shift from mentioning the two incidents to admonishing the two women whom they concern. It is a resumed address that Allah directed to Hafsa and 'A'isha, because the Prophet's ﷺ informing them that he knew what they had divulged was meant as admonition, warning, and guidance toward mending what had been breached of their duty toward their husband. Since that was a sin, for it was a squandering of the husband's rights, and especially by divulging his secret, He reminded them of the obligation to repent from it.

The dual address refers to the one who informed and the one who was informed. As for the one who informed, her referent is mentioned in the speech in His saying (﴿to some of his wives﴾ [at-Tahrim: 3]).

As for the one who was informed, her referent is implicit, because the verb (informed) requires it. As for the informer, her command to repent is evident. As for the one to whom it was divulged, it is because she was a partner in receiving the secret news, and because the one who divulged did not tell her except knowing that she desired a similar exchange. So these are two admonitions: one for the divulger of the secret and one for the one to whom it was divulged in that matter. It was incumbent upon her to forbid the other from that, or to inform her husband of what her co-wife had divulged about him.

"Saghat" means inclined, i.e., inclined toward goodness and the due right of companionship with the husband. From this, hearing speech is called "iṣgha" (attentive listening), because the listener inclines his hearing toward the one speaking to him. This was discussed earlier at His saying, Exalted is He (﴿and that the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter may incline to it﴾ [al-An'am: 113]), in Surat al-An'am. In it is an allusion that in what the two of them did there was a deviation from the etiquette of companionship which Allah commanded, and that they must repent from what they did, so that thereby the rectification of what had corrupted of their hearts may occur.

These two etiquettes, the eighth and ninth, are among the etiquettes which these verses contain.

Repentance (tawba) is regret for the sin, and resolve not to return to it. Discussion of it will come in this surah.

Since the addressee is dual, the plural form "qulub" (hearts) was used with reference to the two, seeking lightness of the utterance when it is attached to a dual pronoun, out of dislike for the gathering of two duals, for the dual form is heavy due to its rarity in speech. When confusion is absent, it is permissible to express the dual by the plural form.

Page 357
This is a usage of the Arabs not following the regular analogy. It occurs in every dual noun that is attached to a dual noun, so the first becomes plural, as in this verse, and in the verse of Khitam al-Mujashi‘i:

*"And two desolate, hollow deserts, both of them with backs like the backs of two shields."*

The most common and most eloquent usage of the Arabs in this is to express with a plural form attached to a dual noun, because the plural form may be applied to two in speech, so they alternate. It is rare to use a singular form attached to a dual noun. Ibn 'Usfur said: it is restricted to what is heard (samā‘).

Abu Hayyan cited for it as evidence the poet's verse:

*"O dove of the two valleys' bottom, sing; may the bright clouds' rain water you."*

In al-Tashil, preference is given to expressing the dual-attached noun by a singular noun over expressing it by the dual form. Abu Hayyan said in al-Bahr al-Muhit that Ibn Malik erred in that. I say: al-Jahiz, in al-Bayan wa al-Tabyin, held that the saying of one who says "buy the head of two rams," meaning "the two heads of two rams," is an error. He said: because that is not the case. End. This supports Ibn 'Usfur's view that expressing the attached dual noun by a singular form is restricted to what is heard, i.e., it is not to be resorted to. Al-Zamakhshari, in al-Mufassal, restricted this expression with the condition that the two words not be separated. He said: the two may be made in the plural form when they are connected, as in His saying (﴿so your hearts have indeed inclined﴾), but they did not say in the separated case: "afrasuhuma" (their horses) or "ghilmanuhuma" (their boys). It has come (in poetry): "wada'a rihalahuma" (they set down their saddles). Thus he differed from Ibn Malik's unrestricted statement in al-Tashil, and the approach of the author of al-Mufassal is more evident.

His saying (﴿and if you cooperate against him﴾) is the opposite of (﴿if you repent﴾), i.e., and if you persist in returning to your conspiracy against him, then indeed Allah is his protector, etc.

Mudahara (cooperation) means assistance; one says "zaharahu," i.e., he supported and aided him. Allah, Exalted is He, said (﴿and they did not assist anyone against you﴾ [at-Tawba: 4]) in Surat Bara'a. Perhaps the verbs of "mudahir" and the description "zahir" are all derived from the non-derived noun "zahr" (back), because the helper and supporter seems to strengthen the back of the one he helps; for this reason, no bare verb has been heard for these derived verbs and the descriptions branching from them. Close to this is the verb "'adada," since they said "shadda 'adudahu" (he strengthened his arm).

Page 358
The original of (﴿tazahara﴾) is "tatazahara," so the tā' was changed to zā' because of the closeness of their articulation points and was assimilated into the zā' of the word. This is the reading of the majority. ‘Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "tazahara" with the zā' lightened, by deleting one of the two tā's for lightness.

"Salih" is a singular noun intended to mean a righteous group or the righteous kind among the believers, as in His saying (﴿so among them is one who is guided﴾ [al-Hadid: 26]). What is meant by (﴿salih al-mu'minin﴾) is the believers sincere, free from hypocrisy and wavering.

The clause (﴿indeed Allah is his protector﴾) stands in the position of the answer to the conditional in meaning, because it conveys the meaning that He will take charge of your recompense for cooperating against him, since Allah is his protector. In this omission there is room in which the listener's mind goes every way in terror.

The separating pronoun in His saying (﴿He is his protector﴾) conveys restriction (qasr) under the assumption that the condition is fulfilled, i.e., if you two cooperate against him, then indeed Allah is his helper, not you two; and your support, which was your duty, is nullified when you failed in it under this assumption. In this is a declaration that Allah is the helper of His Messenger ﷺ, lest anyone after him fall into neglect of his support.

This is the tenth of the meanings of admonition and discipline in these verses.

The conjoining of (﴿Jibril and salih al-mu'minin﴾) in this meaning is an honoring of the status of the messenger of revelation among the angels and of the righteous believers. In it is an implicit reproach that they would be (under the assumption that this condition is fulfilled) from other than the righteous.

These two honorings are the eleventh and twelfth of the meanings I have indicated earlier.

His saying (﴿and after that the angels are supporters﴾) is a conjunction of a clause over the one before it, and its purpose is to magnify this support by the abundance of supporters, honoring the love of the people of heaven for the Prophet ﷺ and the goodness of his mention among them, for that increases Allah's support of him in dignity.

In the hadith: "When Allah loves a servant, He calls Jibril: 'Indeed I love so-and-so, so love him.' Jibril loves him, then Jibril calls among the people of heaven: 'Indeed Allah loves so-and-so, so love him,' and the people of heaven love him; then acceptance is placed for him among the people of the earth."

Page 359
So what is meant by the people of the earth in it are the righteous believers among them, because the one whom Allah loves, He loves for his righteousness, and the righteous are not loved by the people of corruption and error. Thus this verse is explained by that hadith.

This is the thirteenth of the meanings of instruction contained in these verses.

His saying (ba'da dhalika) — the demonstrative in it refers to what was mentioned, i.e., after the support of Allah, Jibril and the righteous believers.

The word "ba'd" here means "ma'a" (with), so the sequence here is sequence in mention, like His saying (﴿Gross, and after that, illegitimate﴾ [al-Qalam: 13]).

The purpose of mentioning the angels after mentioning the support of Allah, Jibril and the righteous believers is that those mentioned before them have manifest traces of their support: revelation from Allah to the Prophet ﷺ through Jibril, and his support by the believers. So Allah alerted the two women to another support whose traces are not manifest, namely the support of the angels with victory on the day of Badr and other than victory, such as seeking forgiveness in the heavens. Thus no one should imagine that this requires preferring the support of the angels over that of Jibril, let alone over the support of Allah, Exalted is He.

"Zahir" is a description meaning "mudahir," i.e., supporter, and it is derived from "zahr" (back). It is of the form "fa'il" in the sense of "mufa'il," like "hakim" in the sense of "muhkim," as was mentioned just before in His saying (﴿if you cooperate against him﴾). The form "fa'il" which is not in the sense of "maf'ul" originally agrees with the noun it describes in its gender and otherwise. If it is here a predicate about the angels, as is apparent, then its singular form is according to the interpretation of the angels as a plural in the sense of a supporting company; or it is the application of "fa'il" in the sense of "fa'il" as the pattern of "fa'il" in the sense of "maf'ul," as in His saying (﴿Indeed the mercy of Allah is near to the good-doers﴾ [al-A'raf: 56]), and His saying (﴿and the disbeliever was a supporter against his Lord﴾ [al-Furqan: 55]), and His saying (﴿and excellent are those as companions﴾ [an-Nisa': 69]). If it is a predicate about Jibril, then (﴿salih al-mu'minin and the angels﴾) is a conjunction over Jibril, and (﴿ba'da dhalika﴾) is a circumstantial clause (hal) of the angels.

In the combination of (﴿Allah made him victorious over it﴾ [at-Tahrim: 3]), (﴿if you two cooperate against him﴾), and (zahir) there are paronomasias (tajnisat).

[Page 360]

This is not connected to the conditional in His saying, ﴿And if you two back each other up against him﴾ [al-Tahrim: 4]. Rather, it is a resumed statement (*isti'naf*), turned toward warning all of the Prophet's wives to beware lest his chest become constricted from bearing the like of this conduct, so that he divorces them. The purpose is that the one who committed it would desist and the others would be warned against imitating her.

The sentence is a fresh resumption (*isti'naf ibtida'i*), following the sentence ﴿If you two repent to Allah, your hearts have certainly inclined﴾ [al-Tahrim: 4]. That sentence conveyed a warning of punishment in the Hereafter if the two of them did not repent for what had transpired between them concerning the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This allusion conveys a warning of a worldly punishment for them, in which Allah commands His Prophet (ﷺ) to divorce them. What follows from accountability in the Hereafter, if they do not repent, is in addition to this. For this reason it was separated from the preceding sentence, because the two aims differ.

In His saying, ﴿It may be that his Lord, if he divorces you, will substitute for him wives better than you﴾, there is brevity (*ijaz*) by omitting what follows from the substitution: the implied meaning is "if he separates from you." The sense is: "It may be that he divorces you, and he only divorces by the permission of his Lord, and that his Lord replaces him with wives better than you."

In this there is an indication of the fourteenth and fifteenth of the meanings of admonition and guidance that we mentioned above.

Here *'asa* (it may be) is used in the sense of certainty, and it is chosen here because this substitution is merely a supposition and not an actuality, since these wives are not thought to fail to refrain from what they have been warned against. In His saying, ﴿better than you﴾, there is a reminder to them that they gained no superiority over women except through the favour of their husband with Allah. And the mention of detailed attributes after the general attribute, which is ﴿better than you﴾, serves to alert that the roots of excellence exist in them. Thus those whom the Prophet (ﷺ) marries have a superiority over the rest of women, in that they became wives of the Prophet (ﷺ).

This verse, up to His saying ﴿better than you﴾, was revealed in agreement with a statement that Umar said to his daughter Hafsa, may Allah be pleased with them both, using a similar wording. This is from the Qur'an that was revealed in accord with the statement or opinion of Umar, as an honouring of his excellence. It has been reported in a hadith in the two *Sahihs*, with the wording of al-Bukhari, from Umar, who said: "I agreed with my Lord in three matters. I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, if only you took the station of Ibrahim as a place of prayer.' Then it was revealed: ﴿And take the station of Ibrahim as a place of prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 125]. And I said: 'The righteous and the wicked enter upon you, so if only you commanded the Mothers of the Believers to observe the veil.' Then Allah revealed the verse of the veil. And news reached me of the Prophet's reproach of some of his wives, so I entered upon them and said: 'If you desist, or else Allah will substitute for His Messenger wives better than you.' Then Allah revealed: ﴿It may be that his Lord, if he divorces you, will substitute for him wives better than you, submissive...﴾ the verse."

This is an admonition: that Allah permits him to divorce them, and that there will come to him wives better than them.

This is an indication of the sixteenth of the admonitions of these verses.

The majority (*al-Jumhur*) read ﴿that He substitute him﴾ with a shadda on the dal, as the imperfect of *baddala*. Ya'qub read it with a single dal, as the imperfect of *abdala*.

*Muslimat* (submissive): those characterized by Islam. *Mu'minat* (believing): those who affirm in their souls. *Qanitat* (obedient): those who stand in obedience in the finest manner. Qunut has been discussed in His saying, ﴿And stand before Allah devoutly obedient﴾ [al-Baqarah: 238] in Surat al-Baqarah, and His saying, ﴿And whoever of you is devoutly obedient to Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Ahzab: 31] in Surat al-Ahzab.

In this attribute there is an indication that they obey Allah and His Messenger. Thus there is an allusion to the shortcoming that one of them had fallen into, for which Allah reproached her and awakened her to repentance.

*Ta'ibat* (repentant): those who desist from sin when they fall into it. In this there is an allusion to renewing the exhortation to repentance for the sin of the two of them, for which they were commanded by His saying, ﴿If you repent to Allah﴾ [al-Tahrim: 4].

*'Abidat* (worshipful): those who devote themselves to the worship of Allah. These attributes convey an indication of the excellence of this piety, which is the seventeenth of the meanings of lesson in these verses.

*Sa'ihat* (travelling): those who emigrate. This attribute was mentioned to alert them that, even if they boast of emigrating, there are many other women who emigrated, and emigrants are superior to others. This attribute points to the eighteenth of the meanings of consideration in these verses.

These attributes are in the accusative as qualifiers (*nu'ut*) of ﴿wives﴾. Some of them were not conjoined to others with the *waw*, in order to explicitly establish all of these attributes for each one of them. Had they been conjoined with *waw*, it would have been possible that the *waw* was of division, meaning dividing the wives into those for whom some of these attributes hold and not others. Do you not see that when it was intended to convey the establishment of one of two attributes and not the other, out of the two qualifiers that came after that, how the *waw* was used to conjoin His saying

[Page 362]

﴿and virgins﴾, because previously-married women are not described as virgins, and virgins are not described as previously married.

I say: in His saying, ﴿submissive, believing, obedient, repentant, worshipful, travelling﴾, there is an embellishment of balanced speech, for a verse of the full *basit*-type metre (*bahr al-ramal al-tamm*) is formed from it: *fa'ilatun fa'ilatun fa'ilatun fa'ilatun fa'ilatun fa'ilatun*.

The reason for this detailed description regarding the prospective wives is that both attributes are esteemed by men. The previously married woman is more attentive to the duties of the husband, more inclined to his desires, more capable in managing his household, sweeter in speech, more radiant in adornment, and more charming in coquetry.

The virgin is more bashful, more innocent, and more coy and graceful. This is an attraction for the soul, and a virgin does not know a man before her husband. Thus in men's souls there is a kind of rivalry over the woman whom no one else has preceded them to.

So no wife of the Prophet (ﷺ) took pride in any distinction except that Allah informed her that He would substitute for him one better than her in that distinction too.

This is the nineteenth of the meanings of admonition and discipline in these verses.

The mention of the attribute "previously married" first is because most of the Prophet's wives, when he married them, were previously married. Perhaps it is an allusion that the greater blame was directed at Hafsa before Aisha. Hafsa was among those he married as previously married, while Aisha is the one he married as a virgin. This allusive reference is a method of discipline, as it has been said: "The free person is sufficed by a hint."

This is the twentieth of the meanings of the lessons of these verses.

Among the curious literary questions related to this verse is that the *waw* in His saying, ﴿previously married and virgins﴾, was claimed by Ibn Khalawayh to be a *waw* with a special usage. He named it "the *waw* of the eight" (*waw al-thamaniyah*). Following him was a group, among whom were mentioned al-Hariri, al-Tha'labi, the exegete al-Naysaburi, and al-Qadi al-Fadil. They claimed that they had derived from the Qur'an that whatever contains the meaning of the number eight, a *waw* enters upon it. It appears from the examples they cited that they consider whatever indicates a thing counted by the number eight to be of this kind, whether it is a derived attribute from the number eight, or a thing that is the eighth, or whether it contains eight, whether singular or a sentence.

They cited His saying in Surat (Bara'ah) [al-Tawbah], ﴿The repentant, the worshippers, the praisers, the travellers, the bowers, the prostrators, those who enjoin right and forbid wrong﴾ [al-Tawbah: 112]. They said: the listed attributes are not conjoined with *waw* except upon reaching the eighth attribute, which is "those who forbid wrong." They counted of this kind the verse of Surat al-Tahrim, since among the attributes beginning with His saying "submissive," none is conjoined except the eighth, which is "and virgins." And they cited as an example of an eighth attribute His saying, ﴿They say: they were seven, and their eighth was their dog﴾ [al-Kahf: 22] in Surat al-Kahf. Thus "their fourth" and "their sixth" were not conjoined, and the sentence in which the description of the eighth occurs was conjoined with the *waw* of conjoining sentences. And they cited as an example of what contains the word "eight" His saying in Surat al-Haqqah, ﴿He subjected them for seven nights and eight days as a continuous destruction﴾ [al-Haqqah: 7]. And they cited as an example of what contains eight names His saying in Surat al-Zumar, ﴿And those who feared their Lord will be driven to Paradise in groups, until, when they reach it and its gates are opened...﴾ [al-Zumar: 73]. They said: the sentence "and its gates were opened" came with the *waw*, whereas its counterpart mentioned before it did not, which is ﴿And those who disbelieved will be driven to Hell in groups, until, when they reach it, its gates will be opened﴾ [al-Zumar: 71]. This is because the gates of Paradise are eight.

Their statements varied as to whether this *waw* is of the category of the conjoining *waw*, which differs from the other category that must be mentioned when the conjoined item carries the meaning of "eighth," or whether it is of the category of the superfluous *waw*.

Al-Damamini, in the Indian glosses on *al-Mughni*, mentioned that he saw in the tafsir of al-Imad al-Kindi, the judge of Alexandria, who died around the year 720, an attribution of the claim affirming the *waw* of eight to Abd Allah al-Kafif al-Malqi, the grammarian of Ghirnata, one of the scholars of Ghirnata in the time of the Amir Ibn Habus, with a *ba'* after the unpointed *ha'*, namely Badis ibn Habus, ruler of Ghirnata, in the year 420.

Al-Suhayli, in *al-Rawd al-Unf*, when discussing the revelation of Surat al-Kahf, mentioned that he devoted a lengthy chapter to the *waw* which some people call the *waw* of eight, but he did not state his opinion on its establishment, and I have not found the place where he devoted discussion to it. It appears that he did not agree with establishing this usage for it. Among the wonders of coincidence is that in these four verses there arose something that gives rise to doubt for those who established this meaning among the meanings of the *waw*. And among the rare cleverness is the alertness of the one who made this known.

Ibn al-Munir, in *al-Intisaf*, mentioned that his shaykh Ibn al-Hajib told him that the judge al-Fadil Abd al-Rahim al-Baysani, the secretary, believed that the *waw* in His saying, ﴿and virgins﴾, is the *waw* which some weak grammarians named the *waw* of eight. Al-Fadil used to boast of extracting it as occurring beyond the three well-known places, until one day he mentioned it in the presence of Abu al-Jud the grammarian, the reciter. He made clear to them that he was mistaken in counting it in that category, and he referred the explanation to the meaning mentioned by al-Zamakhshari, namely the demand for the *waw* to be used here because the two categories cannot be combined in one described thing. Al-Fadil acknowledged it fairly and said: "You have guided us, O Abu al-Jud."

I say: I think that al-Qadi al-Fadil hastened to concede to Abu al-Jud, since he could have said: "We did not commit ourselves to requiring that the counted eighth be independent or a counterpart to something else. We only followed what contains an indication of the number eight."

Al-Tibi and al-Qazwini, in the two glosses on the *Kashshaf*, related that he narrated from the author of the *Kashshaf* that he said: "The *waw* enters upon the eighth, as in His saying, ﴿and their eighth is their dog﴾ [al-Kahf: 22], and His saying, ﴿and its gates were opened﴾ [al-Zumar: 73]. They call it the *waw* of eight, and it is so. But it is nothing." The narrator from him said, when he had recited this passage to us: "Have you forgotten the *waw* of eight at my answer?" (meaning he rebukes them for neglecting that meaning in that verse). That is, it is a good answer. And that is pure error, and it may not be taken from him. End of quote.

I say: this contradicts the explicit wording of his statement in the *Kashshaf*. Perhaps the narrator did not properly express the intent of the author of the *Kashshaf*, or perhaps the author of the *Kashshaf* did not see any contradiction between the necessity of mentioning the two *waws*, since the context requires their mention, and the fact that the item conjoined by them is eighth in mention. For subtle points do not conflict with one another. So reflect carefully.

The discussion of the *waw* of eight has already preceded at His saying, ﴿The repentant, the worshippers﴾ [al-Tawbah: 112], in Surat (Bara'ah), and at His saying, ﴿They say: they were seven, and their eighth was their dog﴾ [al-Kahf: 22] in Surat al-Kahf. It also preceded in Surat al-Zumar and in Surat al-Haqqah.

[p. 365]

﴿O you who have believed, protect yourselves and your families from a Fire whose fuel is men and stones; over it are angels, harsh and severe, who do not disobey Allah in what He commands them, and they do what they are commanded.﴾

The admonition of the Prophet's ﷺ wives was appropriate for alerting the believers not to neglect admonishing themselves and admonishing their families, and so that the preservation of affection among them does not prevent them from giving them counsel, even if that involves some harm.

This is a second address to the believers, after the completion of the purpose of the first address, the address to the Prophet ﷺ, with the words of the Exalted: (﴿O Prophet, why do you forbid what Allah has made lawful for you?﴾ [al-Tahrim: 1]).

The address was directed to the believers so that they would take the Prophet ﷺ as a companion in admonishing their families.

The admonition and warning were expressed by "protection from the Fire" as a figurative usage (majaz, a word used in a non-literal sense), because admonition is a cause of avoiding what leads to the punishment of the Fire. Or it is a metaphor (isti'arah, a comparison in which one term is substituted for another), by likening admonition to protection from the Fire, for the sake of emphasis on admonition.

The indefiniteness of (ناراً, "a fire") is for magnification. A descriptive clause is attached to it: (﴿whose fuel is men and stones﴾), as an increase in warning, lest they become fuel of the Fire, and as a reminder of the state of the polytheists, expressed in the words of the Exalted: (﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are fuel for Hell﴾ [al-Anbiya': 98]) in Surah al-Anbiya'. It is also a way of making the Fire appear terrible, since the stone becomes its substitute for firewood.

The Fire was described with this clause because its content had already been established in the knowledge of the Muslims before the revelation of this verse, through the words of the Exalted in Surah al-Baqarah: (﴿So fear the Fire whose fuel is men and stones, prepared for the disbelievers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 24]), and through what preceded both of them together, the words (﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are fuel for Hell﴾ [al-Anbiya': 98]) in Surah al-Anbiya'.

Al-hijarah (الحِجارَةُ, "stones") is the plural of hajar (الحَجَرُ, "stone") in an irregular pattern, since its regular plural would be ahjar (أحجار). They formed the plural as hijar (حِجارٌ), on the pattern fi'al (فِعالٌ), and attached to it the feminine ending ha' (هاء التأنيث), as they said bikarah, the plural of bakr, and mihrah, the plural of muhr.

The terror of the Fire is further increased by stating that over it are angels, harsh and severe. The clause (﴿over it are angels﴾) to its end is a second attribute.

[p. 366]

The meaning of (عَلَيْها, "over it") is that they are entrusted with it. The sense of elevation conveyed by the particle (عَلى, "over") is figuratively used to mean authority and control, as was mentioned earlier in the words of the Exalted: (﴿They are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5]). And in the hadith: («so there were no gatekeepers at his door»).

(غِلاظٌ, "harsh") is the plural of ghalid (غَلِيظٌ), meaning one characterised by harshness (ghilzah). It is an attributive adjective (sifah mushabbahah, an adjective of quality whose form resembles the active participle), and its verb follows the pattern of karuma. Here it is used metaphorically for harshness of treatment, as in the words of the Exalted: (﴿And had you been harsh and hard-hearted, they would have dispersed from around you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 159]), meaning: had you been severe, they would not have kept company with you.

(شِدادٌ, "severe") is the plural of shadid (شَدِيدٌ). The shiddah (الشِّدَّةُ, "severity"), with a kasrah on the shin, is in its literal sense the strength of a harmful action, and the one characterised by it is shadid. The meaning is that they are strong in dealing with the people of the Fire whom they are entrusted with: one says "fulan ishtadda 'ala fulan" meaning he treated him badly, and "ishtaddat al-harb" (the war became fierce), and "ishtaddat al-ba'sa'" (the hardship became severe). Shiddah is also among the names of misery, hunger and drought.

The clause (﴿they do not disobey Allah in what He commands them﴾) is a praise of them, placed after their description as harsh and severe, to balance what those two attributes might imply of people's dislike of them. This indicates that they are commanded to be harsh and severe in punishing the people of the Fire.

As for His words (﴿and they do what they are commanded﴾), it is an explicit statement of the implied meaning of (﴿they do not disobey Allah in what He commands them﴾). The context of elaboration (itnab, expansive amplification) in praising them called for it, together with the vivid image it evokes of their compliance with what they are commanded. This emphasis is conjoined by a conjunction that implies difference, to highlight this virtue, since doing what one is commanded is a clearer form of obedience than not disobeying; and the difference between the two meanings is taken into account, even though one speaker said both. You may also take the reference of (﴿they do not disobey Allah in what He commands them﴾) to be that they do not disobey in the tasks particular to them that they are charged with, and the reference of (﴿and they do what they are commanded﴾) to be what they are charged with doing to the disobedient in Hell.

He is from the speech of the angels who are over the Fire. Mentioning this statement here is an *istitrad* (digression) that serves to warn against Hell, that it is the abode of the people of disbelief, as God the Exalted said (﴿So beware of the Fire whose fuel is men and stones; it has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 24]),

Page 367
otherwise the context of the verse is a warning to the believers against the destructive sins that lead to the Fire.

The meaning of (﴿what you used to do﴾) is similar to (﴿what you used to do﴾). The particle (*innama*) restricts the recompense to the likeness of the deed for which one is recompensed, a *qasr qalb* (restriction by reversal) that treats them as though they were someone who offers an excuse and asks that his recompense be lighter than what he has witnessed.

*Al-i'tidhar* (offering an excuse) is a *ifti'al* form derived from *al-'udhr*. The pattern *ifti'al* in it indicates the effort of doing the action, like *al-iktisab* (acquiring) and *al-ikhtilaq* (fabricating). *Al-'udhr* is the argument that absolves its bearer from the consequence of a certain deed. The root of *i'tidhar* has no unaugmented verb meaning "to produce an excuse"; what exists is *'adhara*, meaning "to accept the excuse," which has been discussed earlier at God's saying (﴿And those who make excuses among the Bedouins came﴾ [al-Tawbah: 90]) in the surah of (Bara'ah).

[Page 368]

Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 66, verse 8:

﴿O you who have believed, repent to God with sincere repentance. It may be that your Lord will remove from you your misdeeds and admit you into gardens beneath which rivers flow.﴾

The address to the believers is repeated, and their call is repeated. This is the third call in this surah. The one before it was a call to those who admonish, and this is a call to those who are admonished. This style is one of the methods of address that are used to draw special attention.

The believers are commanded to repent of their sins when they fall into them, because this is part of reforming themselves. After they were commanded to keep themselves and their families away from what would thrust them into the punishment of the Fire, since guarding against the Fire is achieved by avoiding what casts them into it, they may be heedless of the misdeeds they committed earlier. So they were guided to the path of repentance, by which they erase the misdeeds that preceded.

This verse refers back to the admonition of the two wives of the Prophet ﷺ, through His saying (﴿If you two repent to God﴾ [al-Tahrim: 4]).

Repentance (tawbah): resolving not to return to disobedience, together with regret over what was committed in the past. It was discussed at His saying (﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words, and He accepted his repentance﴾ [al-Baqarah: 37]) in Surah al-Baqarah, and in other places, especially at His saying (﴿Repentance is only incumbent upon God for those who do evil in ignorance﴾ [al-Nisa': 17]) in Surah al-Nisa'. Its being followed by the preposition (ila, "to") is because it carries the sense of returning, since tāba is the brother of thāba (both meaning to return).

Nasuh (naṣūḥ): one who possesses sincerity.

Nusḥ (nuṣḥ): sincerity in action and speech, that is, truthfulness in intending benefit by it. Describing repentance as naṣūḥ is a figurative usage: repentance in which there is no hesitation and in which there is no intention of returning to the act repented of is treated as a sincere adviser to others. So in naṣūḥ there is a metaphor (isti'arah), and it is not a rational metaphor (majāz 'aqlī), since what is meant is not that its doer is sincere.

The feminine ending (tā' marbūṭah), which would match the feminine noun being described, was not attached to the adjective naṣūḥ because fa'ūl in the sense of fā'il is always singular and masculine.

Most readers recited (naṣūḥan) with a fatḥah on the nūn, in the sense of an adjective, as you know. Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, recited it with a ḍammah on the nūn, taking it as a verbal noun of naṣaḥa, like al-qu'ūd from qa'ada. Al-Akhfash claimed that the ḍammah is not well known, but the recitation is evidence against him.

Among the conditions of repentance is making up what can be made up of what was neglected, such as wrongful acts (maẓālim) against one who is able to restore them. It is related from 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, that repentance comprises six things: regret over the sins of the past; making up the obligatory duties (farā'id); restoring what was seized wrongfully; seeking the forgiveness of those wronged (istiḥlāl al-khuṣūm); that you melt your self in obedience to God as you raised it in disobedience; and that you make it taste the bitterness of acts of obedience as you made it taste the sweetness of sins.

Seeking the pardon of the wronged person (istiḥlāl al-maẓlūm), until he forgives, takes the place of restoring wrongful acts.

Among the completions of repentance is that the penitent enables the punishment to be carried out on himself, such as retaliation (qawd) and flogging. Imam al-Haramayn (al-Juwayni) said: this enabling is obligatory but lies outside the reality of repentance, because if the penitent regrets and intends not to return, his repentance is valid before God, and his refusal to let himself be punished would be a renewed act of disobedience requiring repentance.

This is a sound statement, since submitting to the carrying out of such punishment is extremely difficult for souls, so they have an excuse for shrinking from submitting to it.

[Page 369]

Repentance from one sin is valid without repentance from another, contrary to Abu Hashim al-Jubba'i, the Mu'tazili. This applies to everything other than repentance from unbelief (kufr).

As for repentance from unbelief through faith, it is valid for the forgiveness of the sin of unbelief, even if the person remains entangled with some of the major sins, by the consensus (ijma') of the scholars of Islam.

The sins from which repentance is obligatory are, primarily, the major sins (kabā'ir). Likewise the minor sins (ṣaghā'ir). Distinguishing major sins from minor ones is another question, whose proper place is the principles of religion (uṣūl al-dīn), the principles of jurisprudence (uṣūl al-fiqh), and jurisprudence (fiqh).

However, God graciously favoured the Muslims by forgiving the minor sins for whoever avoids the major sins. This is derived from His saying (﴿Those who avoid the major sins and the immoralities, except for minor lapses﴾ [al-Najm: 32]), and the discussion of it has already passed in the commentary on Surah al-Najm.

If the penitent returns to some of his sins, or to all of them other than unbelief, the scholars of the community differed about this. The view of the People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah) is that repentance is broken by returning to some sins, specifically concerning the sin returned to, and is not broken concerning other sins. And that the return is itself an act of disobedience requiring repentance. The Mu'tazila said: repentance is broken by returning to some sins, so all his sins return to him. Al-Baqillani agreed with them.

There is nothing in the evidences of the Book and the Sunnah that supports either of the two groups.

The hope (rajā') derived from the verb ('asā, "it may be") is used in the sense of a promise issued by the one who bestows favour, by way of metaphor (isti'arah). The penitent has no right to be pardoned for what he committed, since the disobedience has already occurred. Repentance is only a resolution not to return to the sin. But the regret and fear that the penitent feels, which prompted the resolution, indicate the purity of the soul. So God makes His reward for this to be that He erases from him what has passed of sins, as a bounty from God. This is the meaning of the hope derived from ('asā).

The scholars of Islam have agreed that repentance from unbelief through faith is accepted with certainty, because of the abundance of evidence in the Book and the Sunnah. They differed over whether the acceptance of the repentance of a disobedient believer is definite. The majority of the People of the Sunnah said: its acceptance is hoped for, not certain. Among those who held this was al-Baqillani and Imam al-Haramayn. It is reported from al-Ash'ari that it is certain by revelation (sam'), and the Mu'tazila held that it is certain by reason ('aql).

The expiation of misdeeds (takfīr al-sayyi'āt) means their forgiveness. It is an intensive form of the transitive light form of kafara, which is derived from kufr, with a fatḥah on the kāf, meaning covering.
