﴿On the Day when God will not disgrace the Prophet and those who believed with him. Their light will run before them and on their right hands. They will say: "Our Lord, perfect for us our light and forgive us. Indeed You are over all things competent."﴾

(Yawma, "on the day") is an adverbial phrase (ẓarf) linked to (yudkhilakum jannātin, "He will admit you into gardens"). This is a connection that leads to praise of the Messenger ﷺ and the believers with him. It is the Day of Resurrection. This praise of them by the negation of God's disgrace upon them implies, by allusion, that those who did not believe with him will be disgraced by God on the Day of Resurrection. The mention of the Prophet ﷺ together with those who believed is to honour the believers, and it has no connection with the allusion.

Disgrace (khizy) is the punishment of the Fire. God related of Abraham, peace be upon him, his saying (﴿And do not disgrace me on the Day they are resurrected﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 87]). The negation of disgrace on that day entails honour, since there is no intermediate state between them, as His saying indicates (﴿Whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted into Paradise has triumphed﴾ [Al 'Imran: 185]).

In the relative clause (﴿those who believed with him﴾ [Ghafir: 25]) there is an indication that the cause of the negation of disgrace for them is their faith.

The companionship (ma'iyyah) of the believers with the Prophet ﷺ is their keeping company with the Prophet ﷺ.

(Ma'a, "with") may be connected to an omitted element functioning as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) of (﴿those who believed﴾), meaning in the state of being with the thing in the negation of God's disgrace upon them. In that case the generality of (﴿those who believed﴾) is restricted to exclude those in whom the disgrace of unbelief is realised, namely those who apostatised and died in unbelief.

In this verse there is evidence for the forgiveness of all the Companions (aṣḥāb) of the Prophet ﷺ.

Ma'a may also be connected to the verb (āmanū, "they believed"), meaning those who believed in him and kept his company. In that case what is intended is the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ who believed in him and did not apostatise after him, so the verse indicates a virtue of the Companions.

The pronoun in (nūruhum, "their light") refers to the Prophet ﷺ and those who believed with him.

The annexation of (nūr, "light") to the pronoun (hum, "them"), although no prior report about a light belonging to them has preceded, is not a definite annexation (iḍāfat ta'rīf), since the aim is not to define the light or specify it. Rather, the annexation is used here with the implication of its meaning, which is that the light belongs exclusively to them on that day, such that people distinguish it from among the lights of that day.

The running (su'y) of the light is its extension and spreading. This is likened to the hastening of a walker's stride, because it surrounds them wherever they move, honouring their position, just as banners are carried before a commander or a leader, and just as horses are led before a caliph.

The directions singled out for mention are the front and the right, because when the light is before them they enjoy seeing it and feel that it is an honour for them. And because hands are what precious things are held with, and with their hands they pledged allegiance to the Prophet ﷺ upon faith and support. This light is a real light that God makes for the believers on the Day of Resurrection. The bā' (in bi-aymānihim, "on their right hands") is for accompaniment (mulābasah), and it may also mean "from" (ʿan).

A parallel to this was mentioned in Surah al-Hadid, and what we have mentioned here is more extensive.

The clause (﴿They say: "Our Lord, perfect for us our light..."﴾) to its end is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the pronoun in (nūruhum). Its apparent sense is that it is a contemporaneous circumstance: they say this on that day, and their supplication is a request for an increase of that light. In that case the pronoun in (yaqūlūn, "they say") refers to all those who believed with the Prophet ﷺ on that day. Or it may be that whoever's light is less than the light of others who are superior to him that day says this, in which case the pronoun in (yaqūlūn) is taken to be distributive, referring to the groups of those who believed on that day.

Perfecting the light means sustaining it or increasing it, according to the two interpretations mentioned just above. Likewise the supplication for their forgiveness is a request for the continuation of forgiveness. All of this is an act of courtesy with God and humility before Him, like what has been said about the Prophet's ﷺ seeking forgiveness seventy times a day.

With this, the appropriateness of the concluding phrase becomes clear, (﴿Indeed You are over all things competent﴾), which implies the justification for the supplication, as an allusion to the hope that it will be answered for them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 66, verse 9:

﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and be stern with them. Their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination.﴾

When he had made clear to the disbelievers what would befall them in the Hereafter, explicitly through His saying ﴿O you who have disbelieved, make no excuses today﴾ [al-Tahrim: 7], and allusively through His saying ﴿On the Day when Allah will not disgrace the Prophet and those who believe with him﴾ [al-Tahrim: 8], He commanded His Messenger ﷺ, in their hearing, to strive against them and to strive against those who conceal their disbelief behind the outward appearance of faith, namely the hypocrites. This was so that, when the admonition of the punishment of the Hereafter did not affect them, they would fear that the sword's punishment might be imposed upon them in this world, and so they would desist from disbelief and set their souls right. He commanded His Messenger ﷺ to do this only because the disbelievers banded together with the hypocrites after the Prophet's ﷺ migration (hijrah), taking them as their spies and as hands by which they inflicted harm upon the Prophet ﷺ and the believers.

This, then, is a second address to the Prophet ﷺ, commanding him to establish the welfare of the whole Ummah by purifying it of the corrupt, after He had commanded him to awaken those whose negligence concerned some part of the obligation of good companionship with a spouse.

The striving against disbelief is evident. As for the conjunction of "the hypocrites" (al-munafiqin) to "the disbelievers" (al-kuffar), which is the object of "strive" (jahid), it implies that the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to strive against the hypocrites. Yet the state of the hypocrites was ambiguous: none of them openly declared disbelief, none was witnessed to have done so, Allah did not designate to His Messenger ﷺ any hypocrite whose hypocrisy and disbelief he was certain of, nor did He grant him a special, specific knowledge of this, nor did He command him to proclaim it among the Muslims, as is understood from many reports in the narrations.

Therefore the conjunction of "the hypocrites" to "the disbelievers" must be interpreted either as the verb "strive" (jahid) being used in both its literal and figurative senses, namely striving with the sword and striving through establishing proof and confronting the hypocrite with his hypocrisy. This latter is called striving figuratively, as in the Prophet's ﷺ saying: ("We have returned from the lesser striving to the greater striving"), and his saying to the one who asked him for permission to strive: "Do you have parents?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then strive through them."

In my view, the closer interpretation of this conjunction is that it means instilling terror into the hearts of the hypocrites, so that they feel that the Prophet ﷺ and the believers are lying in wait for them. If any sign appeared from one of them by which his hypocrisy became known, he would be treated as a disbeliever in striving, by killing or capture. Thus they would be wary and refrain from plotting against the Muslims, out of fear of being exposed. This verse is then of the same kind as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If the hypocrites, and those in whose hearts is a disease, and the agitators in the city do not desist, We will surely incite you against them; then they will not remain your neighbours therein except briefly﴾ [al-Ahzab: 60] ﴿Cursed wherever they are found; they will be seized and killed with [intense] slaughter﴾ [al-Ahzab: 61].

As for ghilzah (sternness): its real meaning is the hardness of a thing, and here it is used metaphorically for dealing with severity, without pardon or leniency. That is, "be stern," i.e., be firm in carrying out what Allah has commanded against their like. It was discussed earlier at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And let them find in you sternness﴾ [at-Tawbah: 123] in Surah Bara'ah (at-Tawbah), and at His saying: ﴿And had you been harsh and hard-hearted﴾ [Al 'Imran: 159] in Surah Al 'Imran.

And al-ma'wa (refuge): it means the dwelling place, and it is a maf'al form from awa, meaning "to return," because a person returns to his dwelling.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 66, verse 10:**

﴿God presents an example for those who disbelieve: the wife of Noah and the wife of Lot. They were under two of Our righteous servants, but they betrayed them, so the two could not avail them at all against God. And it was said: "Enter the Fire along with those who enter."﴾

This verse follows the statement ﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾ [al-Tahrim: 9]. Its purpose is to threaten them with the punishment of the sword in this world and to warn them of the punishment of the Hereafter, along with what accompanies this of comparing their condition with the condition of the believers. God struck two examples for the two groups, with counterparts in their two situations, so that the admonition would become clearer and the honouring of the believers would become more illuminating. The benefit of mentioning examples has already been discussed in His words (﴿Their likeness is that of one who kindled a fire﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17]) in Surah al-Baqarah.

*Darb al-mathal* (striking an example) means presenting it and clarifying it, and this was discussed at His words (﴿God is not ashamed to present an example, even of a gnat﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26]) in Surah al-Baqarah.

Thus the sentence is a resumed sentence of initiatory resumption (*isti'naf ibtida'i*). This example does not lack an allusion (*ta'rid*) urging the wives of the Prophet ﷺ to obey him, and [indicating] that God's pleasure follows the pleasure of His messengers. The discussion had been about the two wives of the Prophet ﷺ, and their conduct contained a glimmer of opposition, and the two examples contained a hint of their two situations.

The transitive use of *ḍaraba* with the *lam* that denotes cause indicates that the presenting of the example is for the sake of what follows the *lam*. So the meaning of ﴿God presents an example for those who disbelieve﴾ is that He set forth this comparison for their sake, that is, for them to take heed, to consider themselves in light of the one who serves as the example. When it is said *ḍaraba li-fulān mathalan* ("he struck an example for so-and-so"), the meaning is that he intended it for him and informed him of it, as in His words (﴿They did not present it to you except as a dispute﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 58]) and

Page 374

(﴿And We have presented for mankind in this Qur'an every kind of example﴾ [al-Rum: 58]) and the like. The placement of the prepositional phrase with *lam* before the two objects serves to emphasise the concern with awakening those who disbelieve.

So the meaning of ﴿God presents an example for those who disbelieve: the wife of Noah and the wife of Lot﴾ is that God made the condition of these two women a lesson and a warning to those who disbelieve, namely to remind them that God is not turned away from His threat by any diverter. Thus they should not suppose that they have intercessors with God, nor that their place near the House, their maintenance of the Mosque, and their provision of water for the pilgrims would turn away God's anger from them. If they abandon this assumption, they will turn to reflect on how to be saved from His threat by considering the proofs of the call of the Qur'an and the truthfulness of the Messenger ﷺ. For if there were any diverter that could turn God from His wrath, the most deserving of things to be so would be the position of these two women relative to their two husbands, who were messengers of the Lord of the Worlds.

As for the reason for striking the example with the wife of Lot specifically, rather than other relatives of prophets such as the father of Abraham and the son of Noah, peace be upon them: it is because mention of these two women had not preceded. The father of Abraham and the son of Noah had already been mentioned, so that there would be a new benefit in mentioning them. And so that, in mentioning them right after what had preceded of the collusion of the two Mothers of the Believers against their husband ﷺ, there would be a subtle allusion warning against the thought of relying on the noble bond with them for fulfilling the due right of sincerity owed to the Prophet ﷺ, so that the resemblance in the comparison would be stronger. It is related from Muqatil that God, glorified is He, says to 'Aishah and Hafsah: "Do not be in the same position as the wife of Noah and the wife of Lot in disobedience; rather, be in the position of the wife of Pharaoh and Mary." Al-Zamakhshari (in *al-Kashshaf*) clarified this as being of the kind of allusion (*ta'rid*). Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) rejected it, and Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Some people said: in the two examples there is a lesson for the wives of the Prophet ﷺ when their rebuke was mentioned." But this is remote, because the text is that it is for the disbelievers, and this rules it out.

What dispels this remoteness is that the indication by allusion does not contradict the explicit wording. Among the subtleties of restricting it with His words (﴿for those who disbelieve﴾) is that the primary intent is to strike the example for those who disbelieve. This is a precaution against taking the comparison as a likeness in every respect. Precaution through multiplying comparisons is also of this kind, and among it is the stripping away of the metaphor (*tajrid al-isti'ara*).

The story of the wife of Noah is not mentioned in the Qur'an except in this verse. What appears is that she betrayed her husband after the Flood, and that Noah did not know of her betrayal, because God called her action betrayal.

The Book of Genesis in the Torah (*al-Tawrat*) mentions the wife of Noah among those who boarded the ark, and mentions her coming out of the ark after the Flood. Then her mention was dropped when God mentioned His blessing upon Noah and his sons and His covenant with them, and his wife was not mentioned with them. So perhaps she disbelieved after that, or perhaps Noah married another woman after the Flood who is not mentioned in the Torah.

God described the act of the wife of Noah as a betrayal of her husband. The exegetes said: it was a betrayal in religion, that is, she was a disbeliever who concealed her disbelief. Perhaps disbelief occurred again among the people of Noah after the Flood, and this is not mentioned in the Qur'an.

As for the story of the wife of Lot, it is mentioned in the Qur'an several times, and was discussed in Surah al-A'raf. It is said: "So-and-so was under so-and-so," meaning she was his wife.

The verb *kānat taḥta* ("was under") here is a metaphor for protection and safeguarding (*al-ṣiyāna wa-l-'iṣma*). From this is the saying of Anas ibn Malik in the hadith transmitted in the *Muwatta'* and in the *Sahih* of al-Bukhari, from Umm Haram bint Milhan, and Umm Haram was under 'Ubada ibn al-Samit.

Among the excellent answers is that a certain ruler from the Shi'a asked a scholar of the Sunnah (*ahl al-sunna*): "Who is the best of people after the Messenger of God ﷺ?" He answered: "The one whose daughter was under him." The ruler thought that he had preferred 'Ali, because he understood the pronoun attached to *ibnatu* ("daughter") to refer to the Messenger of God ﷺ, and the pronoun attached to *taḥta* ("under") to refer to the relative pronoun. But the Sunni scholar intended the reverse: that the pronoun in *ibnatuhu* refers to the relative pronoun, and the pronoun in *taḥtahu* refers to the Messenger of God ﷺ, and that man is Abu Bakr.

It has become clear that the intended meaning of "the two servants" is Noah and Lot. They were specifically described as "two righteous servants," although prophethood is itself a form of righteousness, in order to honour the attribute of righteousness and to hint that prophethood is righteousness, so that the station of the righteous is magnified, as in His words (﴿And We gave him the good news of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous﴾ [al-Saffat: 112]). And so that the admonition would extend to the women of the Muslims in their treatment of their husbands, since the attribute of prophethood has ended with respect to the Islamic community. This is in addition to the magnitude of the harm inflicted upon the righteous servants of God, and His care for them and His defence of them.

*Al-khiyana* and *al-khawn* are the opposite of trustworthiness (*al-amana*) and the opposite of faithfulness (*al-wafa'*). That is, it is a neglect by a person of what he was entrusted with and what was committed to him. His words gathered both (﴿O you who believe, do not betray God and the Messenger, nor betray your trusts while you know﴾ [al-Anfal: 27]).

The word *shay'an* is in the accusative as an absolute object (*maf'ul mutlaq*) of *yughniyā* ("avail"), because the meaning is "any availing" (*shay'an min al-ghina*). The indefiniteness of *shay'an* is for belittling, that is, the least availing and the most insignificant, let alone significant wealth. It was discussed at His words (﴿They will not avail you at all against God﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 19]) in Surah al-Jathiyah.

The addition of (﴿along with those who enter﴾) serves to indicate that they are equal in punishment with the other disbelieving betrayers. This is a removal of hope for them that they might benefit from the favour of their two husbands, like His words (﴿On the Day We gather them all, then We will say to those who associated partners: "Where are your partners whom you used to claim?"﴾ [al-An'am: 22]).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 66, verse 11:

﴿And Allah presents an example for those who believe: the wife of Pharaoh, when she said, "My Lord, build for me near You a house in Paradise, and save me from Pharaoh and his deeds, and save me from the wrongdoing people."﴾

When the example was given for those who disbelieved, it was followed by the giving of an example for those who believed, so that a comparison would be made and the purpose of the two examples would become clear together. They followed the Qur'an's usual practice of pairing warning (tarhib) with encouragement (targhib).

The example for those who believed was given through the condition of two women, so that a comparison would be made with the two preceding examples. This is an instance of what the scholars call muraʿat al-naẓīr (observing correspondence) in the two examples.

One of the two examples was given for those who believed to show the sincerity of faith (ikhlaṣ al-īmān), and the second example was given for intense piety (shiddat al-taqwā).

Thus the wife of Pharaoh was an example of the steadfastness of the believers, and Mary was an example of those devoutly obedient (al-qānitīn), because the believers disowned their relatives who remained upon disbelief in Makkah.

This wife of Pharaoh was the wife of the Pharaoh to whom Moses was sent, and he was munfaṭiḥ al-thālith, and she was not the wife of Pharaoh who adopted Moses when she picked him up from the river, because that occurred in the time of Pharaoh Ramesses II, and there were eighty years between the two periods. Moreover, they had no knowledge of a religion before Moses was sent to them.

Page 377

It is possible that this wife of Pharaoh was one of the daughters of Israel whom Pharaoh married, so she was a believer in the message of Moses, peace be upon him. Some exegetes have related that she was the paternal aunt of Moses, or that Allah guided her to faith just as He guided the believing man from the family of Pharaoh, whose mention preceded in Surah Ghafir. The Prophet (ﷺ) named her Asiya in his saying: "Many men have attained perfection, but among women none has attained perfection except Mary, the daughter of 'Imran, and Asiya, the wife of Pharaoh." Related by al-Bukhari.

By "the deeds of Pharaoh" she meant his injustice, that is: "Save me from the consequences of his deeds." So the meaning of "save me from Pharaoh" is "save me from his company," which she sought for herself as a means of relief, and this is an instance of mentioning the particular after the general (ʿaṭf al-khāṣṣ ʿalā al-ʿāmm).

The meaning of "she said" (qālat) is that she declared it openly. It has been related that Pharaoh discovered her and announced this to his people, and he ordered her to be tortured, so she died under his torture without feeling pain.

The wrongdoing people are the people of Pharaoh, and their wrongdoing is their associating partners with Allah.

The apparent meaning is that her words "build for me near You a house in Paradise" indicate that Pharaoh and his people had barred her from faith in him, and made her believe that if she believed in Moses she would lose a great kingdom and a magnificent palace; or that Pharaoh admonished her that if she persisted in this she would be killed, so her burial place would not be the pyramid (al-haram) that Pharaoh had built for himself, for burial at the beginning of the kings' reigns. This is supported by what the exegetes have related, that her house in Paradise was made of a single pearl, so it would resemble the pyramid that had been prepared to preserve her body and her husband's after death. Her words are thus like the words of the magicians who believed, in reply to Pharaoh's threat: (﴿We will not prefer you over the clear proofs that have come to us and over He who originated us, so decide what you will decide﴾ [Ta-Ha: 72]), in Surah Ta-Ha.

[Page 378]

It is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) with ﴿the wife of Pharaoh﴾ [al-Tahrim: 11]. That is, God struck a parable for those who believed: Mary, daughter of ʿImran. He struck two parables of evil and two parables of good.

The lineage and honour of Mary, daughter of ʿImran, have been discussed in Surat Al ʿImran and elsewhere.

God mentioned her name in several places in the Qur'an. Ibn al-Tilimsani said in his commentary on ʿIyad's al-Shifa': "God did not mention any woman in the Qur'an by her name except Mary, describing her as His handmaid, to refute the beliefs of the Christians."

Ihsan (guarding, preserving) means making a thing a fortress, so that it is not approached. Its meaning is that she guarded her chastity from men.

The clause ﴿So We breathed into it of Our spirit﴾ is introduced with fa- as a consequence of a reward for the deed that preceded it. That is, We rewarded her for guarding her chastity, by God creating within her a prophet through a means that breaks the normal course of nature. Thereby her mention among the righteous was made eternal.

Nafkh (breathing) is used metaphorically for the swift bringing about of life in what was formed in her womb. The attribution of the spirit (rūḥ) to the Divine name is because the creation of a living being in her womb occurred apart from the usual causes. Or the spirit may mean the angel who is commanded to breathe spirits into embryos. According to the first view, min is partitive (tabʿīḍiyya); according to the second, it is initial (ibtidāʾiyya). The Almighty's saying ﴿So We breathed into her of Our spirit﴾ [al-Anbiya': 91] has already been discussed in Surat al-Anbiya'.

Taṣdīq (affirmation) of her means her certainty that what the angel conveyed to her of God's will, that she would conceive, was true.

Kalimāt Rabbihā (the words of her Lord) are the words that He conveyed to her through revelation.

Kitābih (His scripture) may mean the Gospel that her son ʿIsa brought, and although it was not written down during the time of ʿIsa, the disciples (al-Ḥawāriyyūn) wrote it during Mary's lifetime.

It may also be that by kitābih is meant what God willed and decreed: that she would conceive without a man touching her, and "it was a decree decided" (kitāban maqḍiyyan) [Maryam: 21].

Qānit (devout) means one who is wholly devoted to obedience.

Min may be initial (ibtidāʾ).

By al-qānitīn is meant those who frequently engage in worship. The meaning is that she was the offspring of a righteous people, that is, she followed the path of her forefathers in goodness and chastity.

﴿And does the spear-wood grow except from its own stem?﴾ (a line of poetry)

This is an indication of clearing her of what the slanderous people accused her of.

This is similar to the Almighty's saying: ﴿Good women are for good men, and good men are for good women. Those are cleared of what they say﴾ [al-Nur: 26].

Min may also be taken as partitive, meaning she is one of those who were devout to God. The masculine plural form was used predominantly and He did not say "min al-qānitāt" (of the devout women), following the method of taghlīb (the masculine form prevailing over the feminine). This is bringing speech in accordance with what the apparent situation requires. This verse is an example in the science of ʿIlm al-Maʿānī (the science of meanings in rhetoric).

Its subtle point here is an indication that she is among those who frequently engage in worship, and that such worship is normally associated with men, because the women of the Children of Israel were exempted from many acts of worship.

Describing Mary by the relative pronoun and its clause is because she was known by that attribute from her well-known story, through its repeated mention in what was revealed of the Qur'an before this surah.

In the mention of "the devout" (al-qānitīn) there is an indication of what God enjoined upon the Mothers of the Believers, by His saying: ﴿And whoever of you is devoutly obedient to God and His Messenger and does righteousness, We will give her reward twice﴾ [al-Ahzab: 31], and so on.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "wa-kitābih" (singular). Ḥafṣ, Abu ʿAmr and Yaʿqub read "wa-kutubih" (plural), meaning she believed in the books that were revealed before ʿIsa, namely the Torah, the Psalms, and the books of the prophets from the Children of Israel, and the Gospel, if the disciples had written it during her lifetime.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Surat al-Mulk.

The Prophet (ﷺ) named it "the Surah of *Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion*" [al-Mulk: 1], in a hadith narrated by al-Tirmidhi from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "A surah of the Qur'an, of thirty verses, interceded for a man until he was forgiven, and it is (the surah of *Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion*) [al-Mulk: 1]." Al-Tirmidhi said: this is a hasan (fair) hadith.

This is a naming of the surah by its first sentence, so it is a naming by a clause, as Thabit ibn Jabir was named Ta'abbaṭa Sharran. The word "surah" is in construct with that quoted clause.

It was also called "Tabāraka al-Mulk" by the two words together during the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), and in his hearing, as narrated by al-Tirmidhi from Ibn ʿAbbas: "A man from the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: I pitched my tent over a grave, and I did not reckon that it was a grave, and suddenly there was a person in it—that is, buried in it—reciting the surah (Tabāraka al-Mulk) until he finished it. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: It is the one that prevents, it is the one that saves; it saves him from the punishment of the grave." (A hadith hasan gharib.) So the name of the surah is the combination of these two words, in the manner of counting words in speech, without annexing one to the other, like the naming of *Lam Alif*. A parallel to this is the names of surahs by the disjointed letters that begin them, according to some opinions about their meaning. Accordingly, "Tabāraka" is quoted in the past tense form and "al-Mulk" is quoted in the nominative as it is in the verse, so the word "surah" is in annexation of the named to the name. This is because the purpose is to identify the surah by these two words, quoting the two words that occur at its beginning, while omitting what lies between the two words. This was done intentionally, to distinguish it from *Tabāraka al-Furqān*. As they said: *ʿUbayd Allah al-Ruqayyat*, annexing the whole of "ʿUbayd Allah" to "al-Ruqayyat", to distinguish ʿUbayd Allah ibn Qays al-ʿAmiri the poet from others whose names resemble his, such as ʿUbayd Allah ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUtbah ibn Masʿud; or merely because he became known through the resemblance in the women whose name was each Ruqayyah, and they were three. For this reason, the word "Tabāraka" in this compound must end with a fatḥa. The word "al-Mulk" has a ḍamma on the kāf. This is how it is vowelled in the copy of al-Tirmidhi's Jami', and both are vowels of quotation.

The common usage in the books of Sunnah and the books of tafsir, and in most mushafs, is naming this surah "Surat al-Mulk." Likewise al-Tirmidhi titled it: "Chapter on what has come regarding the virtue of Surat al-Mulk." Likewise al-Bukhari titled it in the Book of Tafsir of his Sahih.

Al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn Masʿud that he said: "We used to call it *al-Māniʿa* (the Preventer) during the time of the Messenger of God," that is, deriving it from the Prophet's (ﷺ) description of it as "the preventer, the saviour," as in the hadith of al-Tirmidhi mentioned just above; and this is not explicit in naming.

In al-Itqan, from the history of Ibn ʿAsakir, from a hadith of Anas, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) named it *al-Munjiyah* (the Saviour). Perhaps that is from his description of it as "the saviour" in the hadith of al-Tirmidhi; and this too is not explicit that it is a name.

In al-Itqan, from the book *Jamal al-Qurra'*, it is also called *al-Wāqiyah* (the Protector), and called *al-Mannaʿah* (the Great Preventer) in the intensive form.

[Page 7]

Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) mentioned that Ibn ʿAbbas used to call it *al-Mujādalah* (the Disputer), because it disputes on behalf of its reciter when the two angels question him. I have not seen this from anyone other than al-Fakhr.

These are eight names by which this surah has been called.

It is Meccan. Ibn ʿAtiyyah and al-Qurtubi said: by the agreement of all.

In al-Itqan: Juwaybir narrated in his tafsir, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn ʿAbbas: "*Tabāraka al-Mulk* was revealed concerning the people of Mecca, except three verses." End of quotation. It is possible that al-Dahhak meant the exception of three verses that were revealed in Medina. This possibility is what the author of al-Itqan's inclusion of this report among the surahs whose verses are disputed seems to imply. It is also possible that he meant that three of its verses were not addressed to the people of Mecca. Under both possibilities, he did not specify these three verses, and there are no three verses in the surah that are not connected specifically to the polytheists. Rather, we find that the first five verses may be intended to refer to both groups, from the beginning of the surah to His saying: ﴿the punishment of the Blaze﴾ [al-Mulk: 5].

In al-Itqan also he said: "There is a strange opinion in it, which he did not attribute, that the whole surah is Medinan."

It is the seventy-sixth surah in the order of revelation. It was revealed after Surat al-Mu'minun and before Surat al-Haqqah.

Its number of verses according to the counting of the people of the Hijaz is thirty-one, and according to the counting of others it is thirty.

Purposes of the surah: The purposes found in this surah follow the patterns of purposes in the Meccan surahs. It begins by acquainting believers with some knowledge of God's greatness and His singular possession of true dominion; and with reflection on the perfection of His creation, which indicates His singularity in divinity. Thereby there is in those verses a portion of admonition for the polytheists.

[Page 8]

Among that is a reminder that He established the order of death and life, so that in both states the courses of the deeds of servants are made manifest in the arenas of competition towards the best deeds, and the outcomes of their courses. And that He is the one who recompenses for them.

And His singularity in creating the worlds, creating them to a degree of perfection fitting for what they are meant for.

Then He followed it with a command to reflect on that, and guidance to His general signs, and those are signs of His singularity in divinity.

Transitioning from that to a warning to people against the plotting of the devils, and their being bound together in the noose of the punishment of Hell; and that in following the Messenger (ﷺ) there is salvation from that, and in denying him there is loss; and an alert to the obstinate opponents of the Messenger (ﷺ) to God's knowledge of what they plot against the Messenger, openly and secretly, and that God's knowledge encompasses His creatures.

And a reminder of the favour of creating the terrestrial world, and the precision of its order, and its suitability for people's lives, in which is their striving and from which is their sustenance.

And an admonition that God is able to corrupt that order, so that people become in distress and hardship, that they may remember the value of blessings by imagining their loss.

He set for them an example of His gentleness towards them through His gentleness towards birds in their flight.

He despaired them of relying on the support of idols, or on them providing sustenance.

He made the state of misguidance into which they had cast themselves seem dreadful to them.

Then He rebuked the polytheists for their disbelief in God's blessing, and for their audacity in making light of His threat, and that it is imminent to befall them.

He rebuked them for their haste for the death of the Prophet (ﷺ), so that they might be relieved of his call.

He warned them that they will come to know their error when knowledge will not benefit them, and warned them of what may befall them of drought and other things.
